verses.zh: 耶和华的默示应验在哈得拉地大马士革―世人和以色列各支派的眼目都仰望耶和华―
verses.en: This is an oracle,[NOTE:1] the Lord’s message concerning the land of Hadrach,[NOTE:2] with its focus on Damascus:[NOTE:3] The eyes of all humanity,[NOTE:4] especially of the tribes of Israel, are toward the Lord,
notes: See note at Isa 13:1.
The land of Hadrach was a northern region stretching from Aleppo in the north to Damascus in the south (cf. NLT “Aram”).

Heb “Damascus its resting place.” The third person masculine singular suffix on “resting place” (מְנֻחָתוֹ, menukhato), however, precludes “land” or even “Hadrach,” both of which are feminine, from being the antecedent. Most likely “word” (masculine) is the antecedent, i.e., the “word of the Lord” is finding its resting place, that is, its focus in or on Damascus.

Though without manuscript and version support, many scholars suggest emendation here to clarify what, to them, is an unintelligible reading. Thus some propose עָרֵי אָרָם (ʿare ʾaram, “cities of Aram”; cf. NAB, NRSV) for עֵין אָדָם (ʿen ʾadam, “eye of man”) or אֲדָמָה (ʾadamah, “ground”) for אָדָם (ʾadam, “man”), “(surface of) the earth.” It seems best, however, to see “eye” as collective and to understand the passage as saying that the attention of the whole earth will be upon the Lord (cf. NIV, NLT).
verses.commentary:
9:1

NASB, NKJV
"The burden"

NRSV, REB
"An Oracle"

TEV
"message"

NJB
"a proclamation"

JPSOA
"A pronouncement"

LXX
"An issue"

This Hebrew term (BDB 672) is used in several senses.

- a load or burden carried by a donkey or camel (e.g., Isa. 46:1-2), used as imagery for people
(e.g,. Num. 11:11,17; Deut. 1:12)

- Levites carrying the tabernacle (e.g., Num. 4:15,19,24,27,49) and, in worship, possibly Levitical
singers lifting their voices

- a heavy prophetic utterance (e.g., Isa. 14:28; Jer. 23:33,34,38; Ezek. 12:10; Zech. 9:2; 12:1; Mal. 1:1)

Zechariah had a message from YHWH he had to deliver. There was a sense of urgency.

▣ "against" This is one of the meanings of this Hebrew PREPOSITION (BDB II 89,
e.g., Gen. 16:12; 1 Sam. 3:9). The negative connotation to Zech. 9:1-2 is supported by 9:3-7. However, it
is not the most common usage and probably if this was the author's intent, another Hebrew
PREPOSITION would have been used (cf. USB, Handbook, pp. 229-230). Zechariah 9:1-2
seem very positive. YHWH's message was not only to Judah, but also to the surrounding nations. It was a
message of hope and forgiveness (cf.Zech. 9:2,10).

▣ "Hadrach" Zechariah 9:1-4 deals with the northernmost geographical areas of the Promised Land
(cf. Num. 34:1-12). This chapter depicts a spiritual invasion by YHWH beginning in the north and moving
south. This first term, Hadrach, appears only here in the OT. It referred to:

- a district near Damascus

- a city in North Syria mentioned in the Assyrian documents (see IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 804)

▣ "Damascus" This was the capital of Syria, Israel's traditional northern enemy
(cf. Jer. 49:23-27).

▣ "as its resting place" This Hebrew term (BDB 629) could mean that

- YHWH's word is focused on His people's enemies

- YHWH's word was resting or abiding in Damascus

The term does not have a negative connotation (e.g., 2 Sam. 14:17; Isa. 32:18). It is even
used of YHWH's resting place in 2 Chr. 6:41 and Ps. 132:8. It is also used in connection with the nations
coming to Him in Isa. 11:10.

▣

NASB, NKJV, NIV
"for the eyes of men"

NRSV, REB
"the capital of Aram"

TEV
"the capital of Syria"

NJB
"for the source of Aram"

NAB
"for the cities of Aram"

JPSOA
"for all men's eyes"

LXX
"the Lord oversees people"

Peshitta
"the ways of men"

This phrase is literally "the eye of man" ("Adam," BDB 9). The focus and attention of

- all human creation will be on the covenant-making God, as well as His covenant people
(cf. Zech. 8:20-23)

- YHWH's care and desire for all humans to know Him and serve Him (cf. Zech. 9:10)

- the inhabitants of the Ancient Near East, especially Palestine, are involved in Alexander the Great's
conquest. He was an instrument in the hand of God (The Expositor's Bible Commentary,
vol. 7, pp. 657-658)

The NRSV and TEV translations require textual changes to arrive at their wording (Adam to
Aram with the addition of "the capital of").

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 和靠近的哈马，并泰尔、西顿；因为这二城的人大有智慧。
verses.en: as are those of Hamath also, which adjoins Damascus, Tyre,[NOTE:1] and Sidon,[NOTE:2] though they consider themselves to be very wise.
notes: For location see Map1-A2; Map2-G2; Map4-A1; JP3-F3; JP4-F3.
For location see Map1-A1; JP3-F3; JP4-F3.
verses.commentary:
9:2 The NKJV adds the word "against" from Zech. 9:1 here (twice) assuming the context refers to
punishment, but TEV links this verse with the phrase "belong to the Lord" (cf. NJB, Zech. 9:1) and thereby
turns it into an affirmation of YHWH's love for the nations. The context, especially Zech. 9:4, favors
NKJV's understanding.

▣ "Hamath" This is a city in the northern part of the Promised Land, which is mentioned in
2 Kgs. 14:28. It is often depicted as the northern-most limit of God's geographical covenant with Abraham
(cf. Num. 13:21; 34:1-12; Josh. 13:5; Jdgs. 3:3). See IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), pp. 804-5.

▣ "Tyre and Sidon, though they are very wise" This refers to the Phoenician coastal cities
mentioned in Ezek. 28:3-5,7 as being proverbially wise. However, judgment came on them because of their
pride (cf. Ezek. 28:2,5-6) and arrogance (cf. Ezek. 28:2,6,9).

Now, the contextual question returns, is this context positive (the nations turn to YHWH)
or negative (YHWH judges the nations)? The Hebrew CONJUNCTION (BDB 453-455) in Zech. 9:2b
has many possible meanings. The TEV has "with"; REB has "for," not "though." Phoenicia was the source of
artisans who designed and built Solomon's temple (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:13-14; 2 Chronicles 2). This could be the
intent of the phrase "they are very wise."

When we look at the following context the same paradox of blessing and cursing repeats
itself. It is obvious that Zech. 9:3-6 are negative, but look at Zech. 9:7-10!

verses.zh: 泰尔为自己修筑保障，积蓄银子如尘沙，堆起精金如街上的泥土。
verses.en: Tyre built herself a fortification and piled up silver like dust and gold like the mud of the streets.
verses.commentary:
9:3 "Tyre. . .fortress" There is a play on the Hebrew word for "Tyre," which is sor (BDB 862),
and the Hebrew word for fortress, masor ("rampart" or "siege work" BDB 848). There was an old city
of Tyre and a new Tyre. New Tyre was an island fortress about a half-mile off the coast, with walls over
150 feet high. It was besieged by several Assyrian kings and finally fell to Shelmanezzar V after a five-year
siege. It was besieged by Nebuchadnezzar II, but after thirteen years it was never taken, Ezek. 29:18,
implies that he gave up. It fell to Alexander the Great in 322 B.C.. in a seven-month siege.
Many commentators speculate that this chapter reflects Alexander the Great's conquest of Palestine in the
330's B.C. as he moved toward Egypt because:

- he destroyed the old Tyre and used the rubble to build a causeway to the island fortress
(cf. Zech. 9:4b)

- he destroyed the island fortress with fire (cf. Zech. 9:4c)

▣ "And piled up silver like dust and gold like the mire of the streets" This is figurative language
reflecting the commercial power of the city of Tyre from their extensive maritime activities (cf. Isaiah 23;
Ezekiel 27).

verses.zh: 主必赶出她，打败她海上的权利；她必被火烧灭。
verses.en: Nevertheless the Lord will evict her and shove her fortifications[NOTE:1] into the sea—she will be consumed by fire.
notes: The Hebrew word חַיִל (khayil, “strength, wealth”) can, with certain suffixes, look exactly like חֵל (khel, “fortress, rampart”). The chiastic pattern here suggests that not Tyre’s riches but her defenses will be cast into the sea. Thus the present translation renders the term “fortifications” (so also NLT) rather than “wealth” (NASB, NRSV, TEV) or “power” (NAB, NIV).
verses.commentary:
9:4

NASB
"the Lord will dispossess her"

NKJV
"the Lord will cast her out"

NRSV
"the Lord will strip it of its possessions"

TEV
"the Lord will take away everything she has"

NJB
"the Lord is going to dispossess her"

LXX
"the Lord will possess it"

Peshitta
"the Lord will destroy her"

There is irony here. The Hebrew term (BDB 439, KB 441, Hiphil IMPERFECT)
means to inherit, but in certain contexts in the Hiphil stem can mean dispossess or disinherit
(e.g., Num 14:12). YHWH wants to include the nations into His family and give them an inheritance, but they
must turn from idolatry and materialism and trust in Him.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

▣

NASB, NRSV, TEV, Peshitta
"cast her wealth into the sea"

NKJV
"will destroy her power in the sea"

NJB
"at sea he will break her power"

NET
"shove her fortifications into the sea"

REB
"will break her power at sea"

JPSOA
"will defeat her forces at sea"

LXX
"will strike its power into the sea"

The question is over the OBJECT of the VERB.

- wealth (BDB 298 #3, cf. Zech. 14:14)

- power (BDB 298 #1)

- fortifications

The NET Bible (p. 1672) asserts that the form can reflect the word "fortress" and that the
chiastic structure supports this root. Alexander the Great used the rubble of the old city of Tyre to
reach the island fortress and then threw (BDB 645, KB 697, Hiplil PERFECT with
waw, "hurl") its walls into the ocean (332 B.C.)

However, as the UBS Handbook notes (p. 234) the Hebrew term can refer to sea power
(cf. NKJV, NAB, REB, NIV). Sea power was the source of Phoenicia's wealth and power.

▣ "she will be consumed with fire" This VERB (BDB 37, Niphal
IMPERFECT) means "devoured." This was predicted in Amos 1:9-10 (cf. Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26)
and fulfilled by Alexander the Great in 332 B.C.

verses.zh: 亚实基伦看见必惧怕；迦萨看见甚痛苦；以革伦因失了盼望蒙羞。迦萨必不再有君王；亚实基伦也不再有居民。
verses.en: Ashkelon will see and be afraid; Gaza will be in great anguish, as will Ekron, for her hope will have been dried up.[NOTE:1] Gaza will lose her king, and Ashkelon will no longer be inhabited.
notes: The present translation presupposes a Hiphil perfect of יָבֵשׁ (yavesh, “be dry”; cf. NRSV “are withered”) rather than the usually accepted Hiphil of בּוֹשׁ (bosh, “be ashamed”; cf. KJV, ASV), a sense that is less suitable with the removal of hope.
verses.commentary:
9:5 "Askelon. . .Gaza. . .Ekron. . .Ashdod" These are four of the five city states of the Philistines
(NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 631-634) in the Promised Land (Gath was earlier destroyed by the Assyrians). The Philistines
invaded Egypt around the 1200's, but were defeated and then settled in the southern coastal areas of Palestine. They
were apparently of the same racial stock as the Phoenicians, possibly from Cypress or the Aegean Islands. They
are the only uncircumcised people in Canaan and were traditional enemies of the people of God (cf. Judges,
1 Samuel). Because of Zech. 9:5-7b, although they are going to be judged, they are also going to be included
in the covenant people (cf. Zech. 9:7c-d). What a surprising message of grace!

▣

NASB, NRSV, Peshitta
"will see it and be afraid"

NKJV
"shall see it and fear"

TEV
"will see this and be afraid"

NJB
"seeing this. . .will be terrified"

LXX
"will see and be afraid"

The NASB has "it" italicized, which means that the word does not appear in the Hebrew text.
From the immediate context, "it" must refer to the siege and utter destruction of the powerful city of Tyre.

Zechariah 9:5 may be an allusion to the prophecy of destruction in Amos 1:6-8 (esp. Zech. 9:8).

▣ "will writhe in great pain" This Hebrew term (BDB 296, KB 297, Qal
IMPERFECT) is used of childbirth (e.g., Isa. 26:12; 45:10) and became an idiom for judgment
(cf. Isa. 13:8; Jer. 30:7; Micah 4:9-10; Matt. 24:8; Mark 13:8; Acts 2:24; 1 Thess. 5:3). This fear and
pain was brought on by the destruction of Tyre, Philistia's northern ally. With Phoenicia conquered by
Greece, Philistia was next!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIRTH PAINS

▣ "Ekron" We learn from Josh. 15:45-47, that Ekron, Ashdod, and Gaza were considered to be in
the tribal allocation of Judah and were its traditional enemy!

▣

NASB
"her expectation has been confounded"

NKJV
"He dried up her expectation"

NRSV
"its hopes are withered"

TEV
"her hopes will be shattered"

NJB
"at the ruin of her prospects"

JPSOA
"at the collapse of her hopes"

LXX
"because it was put to shame by its transgression"

Peshitta
"because her hopoe is confounded"

There is confusion of whether this Hiphil VERB is "be ashamed"
(BDB 101, KB 116, Hiphil PERFECT, cf. Zech. 10:5) or "be dried up" (BDB 386, KB 384).

The second one is found in Zech. 10:11 (Hiphil) and 11:17 (Qal). However, Joel,
which I think is early post-exilic, also has four places where these same two roots are confused
(Joel 1:10,12 [twice] and 17).

If "be ashamed" is adopted then the idiom reflects defeat in battle (cf. 10:5; 2 Kgs. 19:26;
Isa. 37:27; 41:11; Jer. 46:24; 48:20; 50:11-16; 51:45-58; Ezek. 32:30; Micah 7:16), which fits this context.

verses.zh: 私生子（或译：外族人）必住在亚实突；我必除灭非利士人的骄傲。
verses.en: A mongrel people will live in Ashdod, for I will greatly humiliate the Philistines.
verses.commentary:
9:6 "a mongrel race" This (BDB 561) seems to refer to the Assyrian exile of the Jewish people from Israel
(722 B.C.) and the import of pagan people from Media; therefore, this area was populated
by people of mixed national origins.

The rabbis later use this term (BDB 561, an Aramaic word for incest) to describe a child of
the union between a Jew and a pagan (cf. Deut. 23:2-3) or to a child born of rape or incest.

▣ "I will cut off the pride of the Philistines" In this VERB (BDB 503, KB 500,
Hiphil PERFECT) there is a change from the THIRD PERSON to the
FIRST PERSON. This is common in prophecy as YHWH begins to speak for Himself through the
prophet.

As YHWH overthrew Phoenicia (Tyre and Sidon) because of their pride (cf. Zech. 9:2-4;
Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 27-28), so too, Philistia and also Egypt (cf. Ezek. 30:18; 32:12) and Assyria
(cf. Zech. 10:11).

verses.zh: 我必除去他口中带血之肉和牙齿内可憎之物。他必作为余剩的人归与我们的　神，必在犹大像族长；以革伦人必如耶布斯人。
verses.en: I will take away their abominable religious practices;[NOTE:1] then those who survive will become a community of believers in our God,[NOTE:2] like a clan in Judah, and Ekron will be like the Jebusites.
notes: Heb “and I will take away their blood from their mouth and their abominations from between their teeth.” These expressions refer to some type of abominable religious practices, perhaps eating meat with the blood still in it (less likely NCV “drinking blood”) or eating unclean or forbidden foods.
Heb “and they will be a remnant for our God”; cf. NIV “will belong to our God”; NLT “will worship our God.”
verses.commentary:
9:7 "I will remove their blood from their mouth" This may mean that the Philistines will keep the
Jewish food laws (cf. Leviticus 11; 17:10-16; Deuteronomy 14) and, thereby be YHWH's people. Even His
people were accused of eating forbidden, bloody meat (cf. Ezek. 33:25), which violated the Levitical laws.
They were destroyed (cf. Ezek. 33:27-28), but these uncircumcised pagans will be saved.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOD LAWS

▣ "then they also will be a remnant for our God" The concept of "remnant" (BDB 983) is a very
important historical and theological concept. The multiple uses can be seen in the New International
Dictionary of Old Testament Theology and Exegesis, vol. 4, p. 15.

- those who survived a divine catastrophe (e.g., Philistines, cf. Amos 1:8; Jer. 47:4 and Jews,
cf. Isa. 37:4,31-32; 40:11; 42:2; Jer. 25:20)

- those who remain faithful and obedient to YHWH (e.g., Isa. 10:20-22; Amos 5:15; Micah 5:3,7,8)

- those who form the eschatological people of God (e.g., Amos 9:12; Jer. 23:3; 31:7; Isa. 11:11,16)

This is a very strong statement for the inclusion of these hated Philistine enemies who now are also part of
the faithful remnant! Some see this prophecy fulfilled in the ministry of Philip in Acts 8:26-40.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT (three senses)

▣

NASB, NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, JPSOA
"and be like a clan in Judah"

NKJV
"shall be like a leader of Judah"

LXX
"shall be like an officer in Judah"

Peshitta
"shall be like the princes of Judah"

UBS Text Project, p. 411
"like a friend"

The Hebrew term (BDB 48-49) is literally "thousands." It is used in several senses.

- literally (e.g., Gen. 20:16; Exod. 32:28)

- family units or leaders (e.g., Josh. 22:14; Jdgs. 6:15; 1 Samuel 23; Zech. 9:7)

- military units or leaders (e.g., Exod. 18:21,25; Deut. 1:15)

- symbolically (e.g., Gen. 24:60; Exod. 20:6; 34:7; Deut. 7:9; Jer. 32:18)

The difference between NKJV and the others is only vocalization (i.e., vowel points added by
Masoretic scholars). The ancient versions (Septuagint and Vulgate) translated it as "leader," but most modern English
translations have "clan" (cf. Zech. 12:5-6). The NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 407, labels it "Philistine leaders." The contextual
issue is not leadership, but covenant inclusion. This inclusion is all the more shocking when the traditional enemy of
Judah becomes part of Judah!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND

▣ "Ekron like a Jebusite" The Jebusites were the original Canaanite inhabitants of the city
of Jebus, also called Salem (cf. Genesis 14), and later called Jerusalem. When David finally defeated
their stronghold (cf. 2 Sam. 5:6-10; 1 Chr. 11:45-9) he did not relegate them to the sword, but allowed
them to live (cf. Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21; 1 Kings 9:20-21). This Philistine city is now included into
the very heart of Judah—Jerusalem.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JEBUS

verses.zh: 我必在我家的四围安营，使敌军不得任意往来，暴虐的人也不再经过，因为我亲眼看顾我的家。
verses.en: Then I will surround my temple[NOTE:1] to protect it like a guard[NOTE:2] from anyone crossing back and forth; so no one will cross over against them anymore as an oppressor, for now I myself have seen it.
notes: Heb “house” (so NAB, NIV84, NRSV); NIV11 “temple.”

Though a hapax legomenon, the מִצָּבָה (mitsavah) of the MT (from נָצַב, natsav, “take a stand”) is preferable to the suggestion מַצֵּבָה (matsevah, “pillar”) or even מִצָּבָא (mitsavaʾ, “from” or “against the army”). The context favors the idea of the Lord as a protector.
verses.commentary:
9:8 "But I will camp around My house" The VERB (BDB 333, KB 332) is a Qal
PERFECT with waw. This may be an allusion to Zech. 2:5 (cf. Ps. 34:7-8), which
speaks of YHWH's protecting His people (cf. Isa. 60:15-22) in a military sense. The Promised Land had
been invaded again and again because of its strategic location, but there will come a day when YHWH will
personally indwell and protect the Promised Land (cf. Ps. 34:7).

▣

NASB
"because of an army"

NKJV
"because of the army"

NRSV, NET
"as a guard"

TEV
"I will guard my land and keep armies from passing through it"

NJB
"to defend it against all comers"

REB
"post a garrison"

JPSOA
"will encamp"

LXX
"set up a structure"

Peshitta
"cause to dwell"

The BDB Lexicon (663) speculates that this form, which is found only here, is from
one of two roots, "to stand guard" or "to garrison" (BDB 662, cf. NRSV and TEV). However, it also mentions
that the MT notes (Qere) suggest that it may come from another term, "because of a host" or "because of an army"
(NASB, NKJV).

YHWH will protect His new temple.

▣ "For now I have seen with My eyes" There will be no more invasions of the Promised Land because
of YHWH's personal presence and power (cf. Deut. 11:12). This idiom of His all-knowing presence possibly
refers to Zech. 4:10.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

verses.zh: 锡安的民哪，应当大大喜乐；耶路撒冷的民哪，应当欢呼。看哪，你的王来到你这里！他是公义的，并且施行拯救，谦谦和和地骑着驴，就是骑着驴的驹子。
verses.en: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion!Shout, daughter of Jerusalem!Look! Your king is coming to you:He is legitimate[NOTE:1] and victorious,[NOTE:2] humble and riding on a donkey[NOTE:3]—on a young donkey, the foal of a female donkey.
notes: The Hebrew term צַדִּיק (tsaddiq) ordinarily translated “righteous,” frequently occurs, as here, with the idea of conforming to a standard or meeting certain criteria. The Messianic king riding into Jerusalem is fully qualified to take the Davidic throne (cf. 1 Sam 23:3; Isa 9:5-6; 11:4; 16:5; Jer 22:1-5; 23:5-6).

The Hebrew term נוֹשָׁע (noshaʿ) a Niphal participle of יָשַׁע (yashaʿ, “to save”) could mean “one delivered” or, if viewed as active, “one bringing salvation” (similar KJV, NIV84, NKJV). It is preferable to take the normal passive use of the Niphal and understand that the king, having been delivered, is as a result “victorious” (so also NRSV, TEV, NLT, NIV11).

The NT understands this verse to be a prophecy of the triumphal entry of Jesus into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, and properly so (cf. Matt 21:5; John 12:15), but reference to the universal rule of the king in v. 10 reveals that this is a “split prophecy,” that is, it has a two-stage fulfillment. Verse 9 was fulfilled in Jesus’ earthly ministry but v. 10 awaits a millennial consummation (cf. Rev 19:11-16).
verses.commentary:
9:9 "Rejoice greatly" This (BDB 162, KB 189, plus ADVERB 547) is a Qal
IMPERATIVE (cf. Zech. 2:10; Zeph. 3:14,15). This is a shout of joy over the military
conquest by YHWH's Messiah. This rejoicing includes both Jews and Gentiles (cf. Zech. 2:10-13). This
inclusion is so surprising and unexpected (cf. Zeph. 3:14-20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "O daughter of Zion" This idiomatic phrase (see notes at Amos 5:2 and Jer. 46:11) is often
used in judgment passages, but here is an allusion to the love that YHWH has for the descendants of Abraham,
Isaac, and Jacob.

▣ "Shout in triumph" This (BDB 929, KB 1206) is a Hiphil IMPERATIVE.
This phrase is parallel to "rejoice greatly."

▣ "Behold, your king is coming to you" The VERB (BDB 97, KB 112) is a Qal
IMPERFECT. This is one of many quotes in the Gospels which comes from this section of Zechariah. It is used in the
Gospels for Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem (cf. Matt. 21:5; John 12:15). For the concept of YHWH and
the Messiah as King see 1 Sam. 8:7; 12:12.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD

▣

NASB
"He is just and endowed with salvation"

NKJV, LXX
"He is just and having salvation"

NRSV
"triumphant and victorious is he"

TEV
"He comes triumphant and victorious"

NJB
"he is vindicated and victorious"

REB
"his cause won, his victory gained"

JPSOA
"He is victorious, triumphant"

Peshitta
"He is righteous and a Saviour"

This first term "just" or "righteous" (BDB 841-843) seems to be used in several passages
in the prophets to describe the ethical reign of the Messiah (cf. Isa. 9:7; 11:4,5; 16:5; 32:1; Jer. 23:5-6).
The Messiah is called "the Righteous One" in the Suffering Servant song of Isa. 53:11. He is qualified to
reign by lineage and actions.

The term "salvation" (BDB 446, KB 448) is a Niphal PARTICIPLE used in
the sense of someone who is made victorious or someone who is delivered. Both of these terms are used
together in Isa. 45:8; 46:13; 51:4,5.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TITLES FOR THE SPECIAL COMING ONE

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT Term)

▣ "Humble" This word (BDB 776) is used in several ways in Zechariah:

- in the sense of "afflicted" (cf. Zech. 11:7,11; Isa. 14:32; 49:13; 51:21; 54:11) or "poor"
(cf. Zech. 7:10; Isa. 3:14-15; 10:30; 11:4; 32:7; 41:17; 58:7; 61:1). "Afflicted" describes
the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, although Zech. 9:2 and 3 use a different term. Isaiah 53:7
uses the same root (BDB 776 III)

- here, it is the sense of "lowly" or "meek" (e.g., Prov. 16:19)

▣ "and mounted on a donkey, even on a colt the foal of a donkey" Donkeys were the royal mount
of Israeli kings (cf. 2 Sam. 13:29; 16:2; 18:9;1 Kgs. 1:33-34, 38,44). They were a symbol of royalty,
however, the colt of a donkey was used because only the king could ride on this donkey. Therefore, this
would be the first time the colt had been ridden. This entire verse reflects Gen. 49:8-12, which is a
prophecy about the tribe of Judah, but is also a description of the coming Messiah. He will be

- of the royal line of Judah (cf. 2 Samuel 7)

- humble

- a suffering servant (cf. Isaiah 53)

The Gospel writers saw this fulfilled in Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem (cf. Matt. 21:4-9;
Mark 11:7-10; Luke 19:35-38; John 12:12-15).

verses.zh: 我必除灭以法莲的战车和耶路撒冷的战马；争战的弓也必除灭。他必向列国讲和平；他的权柄必从这海管到那海，从大河管到地极。
verses.en: I will remove[NOTE:1] the chariot from Ephraimand the warhorse from Jerusalem,and the battle bow will be removed.Then he will announce peace to the nations.His dominion will be from sea to seaand from the Euphrates River[NOTE:2] to the ends of the earth.
notes: Heb “cut off” (so NASB, NRSV; also later in this verse); NAB “banish”; NIV, CEV “take away.”tc The MT first person pronoun (“I”), which seems to shift the subject too abruptly, becomes third person masculine singular (“he”) in the LXX (הִכְרִית, hikhrit, presupposed for הִכְרַתִּי, hikhratti). However, the Lord is the subject of v. 8, which speaks of his protection of Jerusalem, so it is not surprising that he is the subject in v. 10 as well.
Heb “the river.” The Hebrew expression typically refers to the Euphrates, so the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
9:10 "And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim" Zechariah 9:9 speaks of Christ's triumphal
entry into Jerusalem, while 9:10 describes the Second Coming. Also notice

- YHWH speaks (cf. Zech. 9:6,8) in Zech. 9:10a-c

- the Messiah is spoken of in Zech. 9:10d-f

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARIOTS

▣ "And he will speak peace to the nations" This latter part of Zech. 9:10 seems to reflect
Ps. 72:8-11, where the peace of Palestine is used in a universal sense of the reign of the Messiah.
However, it is significant that the Messiah will speak peace to all the nations as well as the Jews
(e.g., Zech. 8:20-23; Isa. 2:2-4; Micah 4:1-3; 5:4). This surprising, yet prophesied inclusion
(cf. Gen. 12:3; 18:18; 22:16; Exod. 19:5), is the ultimate fulfillment of Gen. 3:15, which relates to all
humanity, not only the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ The last two poetic lines of Zech. 9:10 are parallel in the ideal limits of the Promised
Land (cf. Exod. 23:31; Num. 34:1-12; 1 Kgs. 4:21). "The River" refers to the head waters of the Euphrates.

The phrase "sea to sea" does not seem to fit the universal thrust of this context. Therefore,
it is possible to relate it to "the cosmic ocean," which is universal ANE imagery. See IVP Bible Background
Commentaryr (OT), p. 805 (Zech. 9:10 two items).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

▣ "to the ends of the earth" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND
COUNTRY, EARTH

verses.zh: 锡安哪，我因与你立约的血，将你中间被掳而囚的人从无水的坑中释放出来。
verses.en: Moreover, as for you, because of our covenant relationship secured with blood, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit.
verses.commentary:
9:11 "the blood of My covenant" This is a CONSTRUCT of BDB 196 and 136. This can refer either to

- the original covenant of YHWH with Abraham mentioned in Gen. 15:9-11

- the Mosaic covenant in Exod. 24:8

- This phrase is also used by Jesus in the Upper Room in Mark 14:24.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "I have set your prisoners free from the waterless pit" The VERB (BDB 1018,
KB 1511) is a Piel PERFECT. Apparently this is imagery describing the Jewish exiles returning
from Mesopotamia (cf. Isa. 24:22; 51:14).

verses.zh: 你们被囚而有指望的人都要转回保障。我今日说明，我必加倍赐福给你们。
verses.en: Return to the stronghold, you prisoners, with hope; today I declare that I will return double what was taken from you.
verses.commentary:
9:12 "Return" This is a Qal IMPERATIVE. Zechariah 9:11 and 12 both are
encouragement to the returning remnant (cf. Ezra and Nehemiah). Very few of the Jews in exile ever
returned to Palestine.

This term (BDB 996, KB 1427), however, is often used for repentance (cf. Zech. 1:3,4). YHWH's
people must return to Him, not just to a geographical location or even to an ancient promise. Biblical
faith is personal.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣

NASB, NKJV, Peshitta
"the stronghold"

NRSV
"your stronghold"

TEV
"your place of safety"

NJB
"the fortress"

JPSOA
"Bizzaron"

REB
"citadel"

This term (BDB 131; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 701-2) is found only here in the OT. Its basic root means

- "is cut off" (used of grapes)

- "inaccessible" (used most often for fortifications, e.g., Zeph. 1:16)

- "fortress by enclosure" (cf. Isa. 22:10)

The TEV takes it as imagery for God's care and protection in the Promised Land
(cf. Jer. 16:19; Joel 3:16).

The JPSOA, in its footnote, thinks it is a nickname ("fortress") for Samaria,
the northern capital of Israel destroyed in 722 B.C. by Assyria.

▣

NASB
"prisoners who have the hope"

NKJV, JPSOA
"you prisoners of hope"

NRSV
"O prisoners of hope"

TEV
"you exiles who now have hope"

NJB, REB
"you prisoners wiating in hope"

LXX
"O prisoners of the gathering"

Peshitta
"O you prisoners of the congregation"

The hope is in the covenant-making (cf. Zech. 9:11), promise-keeping, deliverance-giving
God. This phrase is given either to encourage those who have returned or to motivate others to return (NJB).

▣ "I will restore double to you" The VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil
IMPERFECT) is an idiom for something that is complete and full. It can relate to YHWH's
judgment (cf. Isa. 40:2; Jer. 16:18) or YHWH's promise of restoration (cf. Isa. 61:7). YHWH is just and acts
according to His word.

verses.zh: 我拿犹大作上弦的弓；我拿以法莲为张弓的箭。锡安哪，我要激发你的众子，攻击希腊（原文是雅完）的众子，使你如勇士的刀。
verses.en: I will bend Judah as my bow; I will load the bow with Ephraim, my arrow.[NOTE:1] I will stir up your sons, Zion, against your sons, Greece, and I will make you, Zion,[NOTE:2] like a warrior’s sword.
notes: The words “my arrow” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation to clarify the imagery for the modern reader (cf. NRSV, NLT).
The word “Zion” is not repeated here in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation to indicate that the statement refers to Zion and not to Greece.
verses.commentary:
9:13 "I will bend Judah as My bow" This chapter is filled with paradoxes! The coming Messianic peace
is mentioned in Zech. 9:8-11 and yet 9:13 speaks again of war (BDB 201, KB 231 Qal
PERFECT). Possibly this verse shows the promise of Zech. 9:8!

As Zech. 9:10 mentioned "Ephraim" and "Jerusalem," which denotes Israel and Judah, so too,
Zech. 9:13a,b. The divided kingdom will be reunited! As a bow and arrow are used as one instrument, so too,
God's reunited people (cf. Zech. 10:4d).

▣ "'I will stir'" The term (BDB 734 I, KB 802, Polel PERFECT) is used
several times in Zechariah.

- YHWH is aroused from His holy habitation, Zech. 2:13

- the interpreting angel wakes the prophet, Zech. 4:1 (twice)

- YHWH arouses the inhabitants of Zion against the Greeks, Zech. 9:13

- YHWH arouses His sword against His own Shepherd, Zech. 13:7

Two other prophets use this same term in connection with Greece, Dan. 11:2 and Joel 3:6.
Isaiah uses this term often in connection with God directing the history of His people (e.g., "the Medes,"
Isa. 13:17; "one from the east," Isa. 41:2; "one from the north," Isa. 41:25; "Cyrus," Isa. 45:13;
"Jerusalem and Zion," Isaiah 51; 52). Isaiah's use of this term in chapters 51 and 52 may parallel
Zech. 9:13d, "I will make you like a warrior's sword." It is God's strength and purpose, but He chooses
to use human instrumentality.

▣ "O Zion, against your sons, O Greece" The term here for Greece is Jawan or Javan,
which was used originally in the OT for a descendant of Japheth (cf. Gen. 10:2,4; Isa. 66:19), while in
Isa. 66:19 it is used for a nation. In the books of Daniel and Joel, it is used to designate Greece
(cf. Dan. 8:21; 10:20; Joel 3:6). I agree with Joyce Baldwin, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries,
that it is used in its Genesis 10 sense of a distant people on the fringe of civilization, which is how
it is used in this eschatological context (cf. p. 169).

verses.zh: 耶和华必显现在他们以上；他的箭必射出像闪电。主耶和华必吹角，乘南方的旋风而行。
verses.en: Then the Lord will appear above them, and his arrow will shoot forth like lightning; the Sovereign Lord will blow the trumpet and will proceed[NOTE:1] in the southern storm winds.
notes: This picture is part of a larger storm imagery associated with God. Elsewhere the Lord is said to “ride” (רָכַב, rakhav) on the heavens (Ps 68:33), on a cherub (Ps 18:11; parallel to “flying on the wings of the wind”), and on a cloud (Isa 19:1). The Lord also speaks to Job from the “whirlwind” (the same word for storm here). tn The verb הָלַך (halakh) means “to walk” or more generally “to go.” In this military setting it might be understood as marching (ESV, NASB, NIV), attacking (NLV), or sallying, which is making a sudden offensive thrust especially from a defensive position.
verses.commentary:
9:14 "Then the Lord will appear over them" The VERB (BDB 906,
KB 1157, Niphal IMPERFECT) may be an allusion to the promise of protection
in Zech. 2:5 (cf. Zech. 9:8a). It also may be an allusion to Isa. 31:5, where God is a protecting bird of
prey (cf. Exod. 19:4b) or a mother bird hovering overhead (cf. Deut. 32:11; Ps. 91:4). The third possibility
is borrowing the imagery of Assyria where their god fluttered over his troops in battle.

Zechariah 9:14-17 are the hyperbolic language of theophany. The phrases are reminiscent of
other prophetic texts. They are patterned, standard idioms of the ANE (see Plowshares and Pruning Hooks:
Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, D. Brent Sandy).

▣ "His arrows will go forth like lightning" Lightning (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 769) and arrows are often used
as imagery for YHWH's fighting on behalf of His people (cf. Ps. 18:14; 144:6; Hab. 3:11). The concept of YHWH's arrows
being like lightning is found in Ps. 7:12-13, where it may refer to arrows set on fire to incinerate wooden
defenses.

▣ "the Lord God" This is the combination of the Hebrew term YHWH
(BDB 217) and adon (BDB 10). Because it would be repetitive in English to say "Lord, LORD," when
these two terms appear together (so too, YHWH and Elohim, e.g., Zech. 9:16 and Gen. 2:4). They are
translated, "Lord God."

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C., D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

▣ "blow the trumpet" "Trumpet" (shofar) has an uncertain etymology. It came to be used
in Hebrew for a ram's horn (BDB 1051; NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 68). The rabbis designated it to be made (softened and
lengthened by soaking it in water) from the left horn of a male goat. It is used for

- military purposes, Josh. 6:4,5,20; Jdgs. 7:8,16

- religious purposes, Exod. 19:13,16,19; Lev. 25:9; 2 Sam. 6:15; 2 Chr. 15:14; Ps. 81:3; 98:6; 150:3

- information gathering (usually about military matters), Jdgs. 3:27; 6:34; 1 Sam. 13:3

- coronation of a king, 1 Kgs. 1:34,39; Ps. 47:5

- invasion of the land, Jer. 4:5; 6:1; Hosea 5:8; 8:1; Joel 2:1; Amos 2:2; 3:6; Zeph. 1:16

Notice in this context it is YHWH who blows (i.e., "sounds," BDB 1075, Qal
IMPERFECT) the trumpet (cf. Isa. 27:13; Matt. 24:31; 1 Cor. 15:52; 1 Thess. 4:16;
Rev. 11:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

▣ "the storm winds of the south" This could be a reference to

- the Siniatic covenant (cf. Exodus 24)

- God's presence as a desert storm (cf. Isa. 29:6; Ezek. 1:4; 13:11,13)

- "the south" being the antonym to "the north," which was imagery for invasion

The south is often imagery for salvation and deliverance (cf. Jdgs. 5:4-5; Hab. 3:3).

verses.zh: 万军之耶和华必保护他们；他们必吞灭仇敌，践踏弹石。他们必喝血呐喊，犹如饮酒；他们必像盛满血的碗，又像坛的四角满了血。
verses.en: The Lord of Heaven’s Armies will guard them, and they will prevail and overcome with sling stones. Then they will drink and will become noisy like drunkards,[NOTE:1] full like the sacrificial basin or like the corners of the altar.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “they will drink and roar as with wine”; the LXX (followed here by NAB, NRSV) reads “they will drink blood like wine” (referring to a figurative “drinking” of the blood of their enemies).

The whole setting is eschatological as the intensely figurative language shows. The message is that the Lord will assume his triumphant reign over all the earth and will use his own redeemed and renewed people Israel to accomplish that work. The imagery of v. 15 is the eating and drinking of the flesh and blood of God’s enemies, that is, Israel’s complete mastery of them. Like those who drink too much wine, the Lord’s warriors will be satiated with the blood of their foes and will exult as though drunk.
verses.commentary:
9:15 "The Lord of hosts will defend them" God Himself will act on His
people's behalf. His victory is their victory. The term "hosts" in this context would refer to the angelic
army at YHWH's command. See
SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

The VERB "defend" (BDB 170, KB 199, Hiphil IMPERFECT)
can be translated "cover," "surround," or "defend" (cf. Zech. 12:8). In Isa. 31:5 it is used of a mother
bird protecting her young (cf. Deut. 32:11; Ps. 91:4). Here it is used as a shield protecting the soldiers
from projectiles.

▣ "the sling stones" These were stones used in sling weapons (BDB 887 I; NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 930-932)
which were used to defend cities and forts (cf. Jdgs. 20:16; 1 Sam. 17:40,50; 2 Chr. 26:14; Job 41:28). This is imagery for
the complete destruction of a military foe.

▣ "they will drink and be boisterous as with wine" Both VERBS (BDB 1059,
KB 1667 and BDB 242, KB 250) are Qal PERFECTS. This refers to the victory celebration
of God's soldiers (cf. Ps. 78:65).

The UBS Text Project, p. 413, gives three options for this phrase.

- "and they will drink, roar" ‒ ושׁתו המו

- "and they will drink their blood" ‒ ושׁתו דמם

- "and they will drink blood" ‒ שׁתו דם

It gives a "C" rating to option #1. The VERB (BDB 242, KB 250, Qal PERFECT
can mean

- be turbulent

- growl

- murmur

Jews would be appalled at the thought of "drinking blood" (some LXX MSS) but they would be
well aware of loud military victory parties!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

▣ "filled like a sacrificial basin" English translations differ on how to understand
these last two poetic lines. They seem to refer to the previous line about God's people rejoicing with
wine over His victory (i.e., another Qal PERFECT with waw VERB,
BDB 569, KB 583). The wine reminded our author about

- the blood of the slain enemies, captured in a bowl

- blood as an aspect of sacrifice to YHWH

The corners of the altar are where the blood in the bowl was poured out at the base of the
altar of sacrifice.

YHWH made a blood covenant with the descendants of Abraham (cf. Zech. 9:11). Now He defends
them by spilling the blood of their enemies.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SACRIFICIAL ALTAR

verses.zh: 当那日，耶和华―他们的　神必看他的民如群羊，拯救他们；因为他们必像冠冕上的宝石，高举在他的地以上（或译：在他的地上发光辉）。
verses.en: On that day the Lord their God will deliver them as the flock of his people, for they are the precious stones of a crown sparkling over his land.
verses.commentary:
9:16 "the Lord their God will save them in that day" This is parallel
to the opening lines of Zech. 9:14 and 15. As 9:14 had Adon YHWH, this verse has YHWH Elohim.

The term "save" (BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil PERFECT) includes several
connotations from the context:

- military victory

- spiritual renewal and inclusion

- God's personal care, protection, and provision

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT TERM)

▣ "As the flock of His people" This whole section of Zechariah reflects Jer. 31:10-14. God is
the shepherd (e.g. Psalm 23) who acts on behalf of His flock. Later in this section of Zechariah the Messiah
will be described as the wounded shepherd (cf. chapters 12-13) and His people as the afflicted flock
(cf. chapter 11).

▣ "as the stones of a crown" This may be

- a contrast to the sling stones mentioned in Zech. 9:15

- an allusion to Isa. 62:3, the precious stones used to describe God's people

- an allusion to the coronation of the new king (the Messiah as YHWH's representative)

▣

NASB
"Sparkling in His land"

NKJV
"Lifted like a banner over His land"

NRSV
"they shall shine on his land"

TEV
"they will shine in his land"

NJB
"sparkle over his country"

REB
"which sparkle all about his land"

JPSOA
"like crown jewels glittering on His soil"

LXX
"sacred stones roll on his land"

Peshitta
"for they were holy stones cast upon his land"

The VERB in the Hithpoel stem is rare and ambiguous.

- BDB ‒ "to be high," "conspicuous," "prominent" (BDB 651 II)

- Lexicon, William Holladay, "rally around the banner" (p. 240). This comes from Ps. 60:4,
which may refer to Exod. 17:15 or possibly Isa. 62:10.

- KB ‒ "to assemble under the banner" (KB 704)

- "sparkle," "glitter," "shine" are the most common English translations (cf. Isa. 62:3)

verses.zh: 他的恩慈何等大！他的荣美何其盛！五谷健壮少男；新酒培养处女。
verses.en: How precious and fair![NOTE:1] Grain will make the young men flourish, and new wine the young women.
notes: This expostulation best fits the whole preceding description of God’s eschatological work on behalf of his people. His goodness is especially evident in his nurturing of the young men and women of his kingdom.
verses.commentary:
9:17 As the previous verses may be an allusion to Jer. 31:10-11, so too, this may refer to the
return from exile, but extends it to the eschatological future and the time of the "new covenant"
(cf. Jer. 31:31-34).

The promised days of abundance and stability for an obedient covenant people
(cf. Lev. 26 and Deut. 27-29; Ezek. 36:22-36) have now been realized by the gracious actions of YHWH, not
human performance (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36).

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This begins a new section of the book. Zechariah 9:2-11:3 is in a poetic format (NASB, NKJV, NRSV,
NJB). As chapters 1- 8 are dated specifically and the author is specified (cf. Zech. 1:1),
chapters 9-14 are undated and the author's name is not mentioned. This pattern is common in the
prophetic books.

- Isaiah 1-39 and 40-66

- Ezekiel 1-39 and 40-48

- Daniel 1-6 and 7-12

- Zechariah chapters 1-8 are quoted often in the book of the Revelation, while Zechariah, chapters 9-14
are quoted often in the Gospels. Zechariah had an important theological message which still has
relevance.

- This chapter, so it seems to me, depicts YHWH as invading Palestine from the north in an
eschatological sense. His invasion is for spiritual renewal and reunification, not only of Judah
and Israel, but also the surrounding ancient enemies (Hadrach, Syria, Phoenicia, and Philistia).

- It is possible from this passage to see YHWH coming in judgment in Zech. 9:1, 4-8. Many commentators
see these verses as referring to Alexander's conquest of Syria, Phoenicia, and Philistia, but his
sparing of Jerusalem in the early 330's B.C.. If this is so then Zech. 9:1 involves
all men of the area watching the coming of Alexander as God's instrument of judgment.

- In his commentary on Zechariah H. C. Leupold assumes that Zech. 9:1-10 reflect the conquest of
Alexander the Great of Palestine in the 330's B.C., while Zech. 9:11-17 reflect the
Maccabean period, 168-165 B.C. The historical setting is uncertain; possibly it is
a prophetic collage of:

- the past

- the post-exilic present

- the eschatological future

- There are dramatic theological-historical paradoxes in this chapter.

- destruction of the surrounding nations versus their inclusion in the covenant people

- the reference to peace in Zech. 9:8-10 versus a great war of Zech. 9:13-15

- the first coming of the Messiah in Zech. 9:9 versus the second coming of the Messiah in
Zech. 9:10.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ZECHARIAH 9:1-10

1The burden of the word of the Lord is against the
land of Hadrach, with Damascus as its resting place (for the eyes of men, especially of all the tribes of Israel, are toward the Lord),

2And Hamath also, which borders on it;

Tyre and Sidon, though they are very wise.

3For Tyre built herself a fortress

And piled up silver like dust,

And gold like the mire of the streets.

4Behold, the Lord will dispossess her

And cast her wealth into the sea;

And she will be consumed with fire.

5Ashkelon will see it and be afraid.

Gaza too will writhe in great pain;

Also Ekron, for her expectation has been confounded.

Moreover, the king will perish from Gaza,

And Ashkelon will not be inhabited.

6And a mongrel race will dwell in Ashdod,

And I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.

7And I will remove their blood from their mouth

And their detestable things from between their teeth.

Then they also will be a remnant for our God,

And be like a clan in Judah,

And Ekron like a Jebusite.

8But I will camp around My house because of an army,

Because of him who passes by and returns;

And no oppressor will pass over them anymore,

For now I have seen with My eyes.

9Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion!

Shout in triumph, O daughter of Jerusalem!

Behold, your king is coming to you;

He is just and endowed with salvation,

Humble, and mounted on a donkey,

Even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

10I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim

And the horse from Jerusalem;

And the bow of war will be cut off.

And He will speak peace to the nations;

And His dominion will be from sea to sea,

And from the River to the ends of the earth.
